awd_titl_txt: Travel: NSF Student Travel Grant for 2024 Women in Hardware and Systems Security (WISE) Workshop
awd_abstract_narration:
This award will partially fund 10 students to attend the 2024 Women in Hardware and Systems Security (WISE) Workshop.  Hardware and systems security is a critical social issue given society's reliance on microelectronics that are targets of malicious attackers.  To increase the number, quality, and diversity of hardware and systems security researchers, the WISE workshop series provides intellectual, mentoring, and professional network development activities for researcher entering the field.  The series offers a platform for the exchange of innovative ideas around hardware and systems security, as well as panel discussions of the professional challenges of succeeding in this research area.  Students will also have the opportunity to present posters about their own work to both the WISE workshop and the co-located IEEE International Symposium on Hardware Oriented Security and Trust (HOST).

Through these efforts, the WISE workshop series will broaden participation in hardware and systems security, in turn increasing the size and quality of the workforce.  Students' work will also be disseminated through the WISE YouTube channel, increasing awareness of hardware and systems security advances for both the research community and the general public.  Students will be selected based on financial need, the relevance of their research to the field of hardware and systems security, and their career stage (with consideration given to both first-time attendees and to attendees about to enter the job market).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project supported student participation in the 2024 Women in Hardware and Systems Security WISE Workshop, a national event focused on advancing research and workforce development in hardware and systems security HSS. The primary goal was to broaden participation in this critical field by enabling students, especially women and individuals from underrepresented groups, to engage in technical discussions, networking, and professional development opportunities.

Through this award, travel grants were provided to students who otherwise lacked sufficient financial resources to attend the workshop held at the IBM T.J. Watson Research Center in New York. A total of 34 participants attended the event, and 9 students received travel support. The funded students represented diverse ethnic, national, and academic backgrounds, including undergraduate and graduate students, as well as several first time attendees at a professional research event. By lowering financial barriers, the project enabled broader access to a high impact research and mentoring environment.

From an intellectual merit perspective, the project contributed to the advancement of hardware and systems security by facilitating the exchange of current research ideas. A total of 20 student posters were presented, covering topics such as hardware Trojans, side channel attacks, secure system design, and machine learning for security. These presentations encouraged collaboration, critical feedback, and the development of new research directions. The workshop also included tutorials, panel discussions, and technical talks, which further strengthened the knowledge and research capacity of participants.

The broader impacts of the project are significant. The workshop created an inclusive and supportive space where female students could connect with faculty, industry professionals, and peers. Participants benefited from role models who shared their experiences in research and professional careers, helping to build confidence and motivation. The presence of industry leaders from organizations such as IBM, Intel, and Texas Instruments provided valuable insights into real world applications and career opportunities in hardware security.

In addition, the project contributed to workforce development by equipping students with technical, communication, and networking skills essential for careers in science and engineering. Activities such as poster presentations, panel participation, and informal discussions allowed students to improve their research communication abilities and establish professional connections. Outreach efforts through academic networks and professional organizations also helped expand awareness and participation in the field.

The University of Kansas benefited by leading the travel grant management process, demonstrating its ability to coordinate national level educational and research initiatives. This strengthened institutional visibility and fostered new collaborations.

Overall, the project advanced both the field of hardware and systems security and the development of a diverse and skilled workforce, helping ensure that future innovations in secure computing reflect a broad range of perspectives.
